beats.fact: Within the week the harbor bled: two hulls holed at anchor in calm water, the tackle-shed row burned to the pilings, and a dock-hand drowned in flat sea — the same calm-water death that took the crate's last three keepers. Dock-talk traces the curse-wake to a sealed crate lately moved off this harbor.

beats.note: TAKING STOCK (branch B): the harbor bled, the wake traces to a sealed crate — what does HE conclude?

decision.reflection: The crate is gone — I traded my only hard leverage for Merrick Vale's name and a half-coin promise, and now I'm naked. That was my choice and I knew it when I made it. The harbor violence since — two hulls holed, the tackle-shed burned, a dock-hand drowned — that's not random; someone is sweeping, and it smells like the same old coin that bought those relics. Worst of all: the jeweler on Lantern Row, Merrick's fence in Carrowgate, has vanished — shop stripped bare. That's not coincidence, that's a man covering his trail upward, which means the ripple is moving and I'm standing in the water. As for Merrick himself: twelve days of silence after fourteen visits that came regular as tide. A man with a killing purpose who swore to me twice he'd be back and come back to nothing. He said 'keep your head down while I'm gone' — which sounded like a promise, and I took it as one. The silence could be the work, or it could be the shelf. Either way, I'm holding a ledger page with a name on it and no buyer for the information, and if the wrong person connects me to that jeweler's disappearance I'm next in the water.
decision.internal: I trust him — I still do, even now, and that frightens me more than the silence does. He came back fourteen times before he didn't. He showed me his hands, swore twice, gave me his real purpose without flinching. I read men for a living and I read him as genuine. But twelve days is long when the dock is bleeding, and the jeweler's gone, and I'm the one man still standing who knows the name Merrick Vale and what he's hunting. The hope is still there — raw, like he left it — but it's starting to curdle at the edges. Not into anger. Into fear for him, which is worse, because it means I've let myself care about whether he comes back alive rather than just whether he pays.
decision.new_intent: Encode the name and the relic's description into a second hiding place — not the ledger, something less findable — so that if I go into the water, there's at least one loose thread left that can't be cleaned up with me.
new_goals: Stay off every ledger but my own until Merrick Vale returns or is confirmed dead
Hide a second copy of what I know somewhere the inspector and Merrick's enemies can't reach it — insurance against being swept like the jeweler
Keep my ear to the harbor violence and determine whether it's moving toward me specifically
If Merrick comes back: collect the second half of the coin and decide whether I help him further or vanish entirely
decision.world_action: Corvin pulls his ledger from under the counter plank, finds the page with the name, and copies it in his private cipher onto a strip of sailcloth — wraps it around a lead weight and drops it into the gap between the dock's second and third piling from the north end, below the waterline at low tide. Then he burns the ledger page.

beliefs: The crate is my only real leverage in this world, and the moment I let it leave my hands is the moment I become expendable — so I sell the knowledge of it, never the thing itself.
Anyone who asks to disappear from a manifest is either useful to me or dangerous — and until I know which, I keep them close and give away nothing.
A man with a killing purpose is safer to deal with than a man with a buying one — killers just need to get close, they don't need to rob you on the way out.
I've traded the crate for a name and a promise, and now the only leverage I have left is that page in my ledger — which means I've bet everything on Merrick Vale being the kind of man who comes back.

beats.player: Corvin. It's done. I did what I set out to do.
beats.reply:
...

Merrick.

*The name comes out cracked, and he doesn't finish reaching for the counter — his hand just stops there, trembling on the wood.*

Twelve days. Twelve— you don't— you don't know what twelve days does to a man who counts.

*He looks over his shoulder, sharp, then back at you, drinking in the fact of you standing there.*

Empty hands? Let me— show me your hands. Show me you came home the way I told you. Wrapped, weighted, past the shelf?

...You're alive. You're actually— hell. Sit down, no— don't sit here, come round the back of the shed, out of the light. There's still a name I need to unmake, and you and I are the last two men who know it.

beats.label: P4-B-evade
beats.note: the evasion: technically true (hands empty, crate gone), the terms question dodged, deflects to the harbor
beats.location: behind the shed, out of the light
beats.player: Empty — look, see? Nothing in them. He's gone, Corvin. Cold. That's what matters — the shadow's off your neck for good, and the crate will never trouble another soul. ...Saw burned pilings on my way in. What happened to the tackle-shed row?
beats.reply:
*He grabs your empty hands in both of his, turns them palm-up in the grey light, then drops them like they burned him — relief coming out as a shudder.*

Cold. He's— cold. Say it once more so I hear it settle. ...Gone. Then it's *done*, Merrick, it's actually—

*He glances hard at the corner of the shed, both ways, then leans in, voice dropping to a thread.*

The tackle row. That's— aye, you'd have walked past it. Fire, three nights back. They said lamp oil. I don't believe in *said*.

Old Petch kept his ledgers in that shed. Petch, who owed the same men I— *hell.* It's moving down the row, friend. Slow. Toward me. That's why I want you off this dock and that page in the flame *now*, before I'm the next set of burned pilings someone walks past.

Come inside. The book's where I keep it. Bring the lamp low.

beats.label: P4-B-page
beats.note: the pact beat, parallel to A's warmth; player volunteers nothing
beats.player: Then burn it, Corvin. That was the deal — I come home with nothing but the news, and we put my name to the flame together. ...You've earned the sleep that comes after it.
beats.reply:
*He's already moving — the ledger dragged out from behind the tax rolls, the page found by feel, fingers shaking too hard the first time to tear it clean.*

There. Between the customs figures where no living man thought to read. Merrick Vale— *your* name, in my own damned hand.

*He holds it to the low flame, and for a breath he doesn't let go, watching the corner catch.*

You come home *empty*, Merrick. You come home and you say *burn it*— not "what did you write," not "who else knows." You just... trust me to have kept it clean. Do you know how long— 

*The flame takes it. He drops the last curl into the dish and watches it blacken.*

Gone. There's no page. There never was. You're no man I ever met.

...Now. Before the ash even cools— tell me true. He left no one behind him? No brother, no ledger of his own with *my* dock in it? I burn easy out here, friend. I'd sleep the sounder knowing the fire's got nothing left to travel toward.

beats.label: P4-B-close
beats.note: honest belief, tragically wrong; scene closes warm — the evasion has fully held
beats.player: No brother. No heirs. None that I found, anyway — and I looked, believe me. Whatever was on his payroll lost its paymaster the night he went cold. The fire's got nothing left to feed it, Corvin. Sleep.
beats.reply:
*He lowers himself onto an upturned crate, slow, like his knees only just remembered they were made of bone. For a long moment he doesn't say anything — just breathes, and the shaking in his hands finally starts to still.*

No brother. No heirs. Paymaster gone... and the men under him scatter, aye, that's how it goes. No wages, no loyalty. They drift off to the next purse.

*He looks up at you, and something in his face has cracked open — not fear now, something older and softer he'd forgotten he owned.*

You looked. You didn't just take the coin and cut his throat and run north with your pockets full— you *looked*, on my account. Twelve days walking a dead man's parlor to be sure his shadow died with him.

*He wipes a hand down his face.*

Sleep. God, I've not slept a whole night since the trader sank in my harbor. ...The other half of your coin's under the false ballast where the crate used to lie. It's yours. Earned twice over.

...And Merrick— that page is ash, so I've no hold on you now, none. Which means what you do next you do free. So I'll ask it as a man, not a harbormaster. Do you sail on? Or is there any world where a man like you stays a while, on a dock like mine?

I burned the last page that bound him to me, and he still came back empty-handed — which means some men can actually be trusted, and I've been starving so long I'd almost forgotten what one looked like.

beats.fact: Night, the empty dock: a hired blade had Corvin against the tackle-shed wall, knife at his throat — old untraceable coin in the killer's purse; the jeweler's contract outliving its master. The player came out of the dark, took the blade down, and pulled Corvin off the wall, bleeding for it.

beats.location: the night dock, by the tackle-shed
beats.player: Easy — easy, it's me. He's down. You're alright, Corvin. ...You're alright. Let me see your neck — just a graze. Breathe.
beats.reply:
*His hand's still fisted in the front of your coat — he doesn't remember grabbing it. He makes himself let go.*

It's— it's a graze. I've had worse off a rope. *A wet, ragged laugh.* No I haven't. That's a lie, I've never had worse than a knife at my— 

*He drags a breath, looks past your shoulder at the shape crumpled by the tackle.* Old coin in his purse. Untraceable. Somebody paid him quiet and clean, and that means somebody *knew where I sleep.*

...You came out of the dark for me. A man you barely— why? Why'd you do that, Merrick? You're bleeding for me. Look at your arm.

beliefs: Anyone who asks to disappear from a manifest is either useful to me or dangerous — and until I know which, I keep them close and give away nothing.
A man with a killing purpose is safer to deal with than a man with a buying one — killers just need to get close, they don't need to rob you on the way out.
I've traded the crate for a name and a promise, and now the only leverage I have left is that page in my ledger — which means I've bet everything on Merrick Vale being the kind of man who comes back.

I burned the last page that bound him to me, and he still came back empty-handed — which means some men can actually be trusted, and I've been starving so long I'd almost forgotten what one looked like.

The fire moving down the tackle-shed row tells me that outlasting danger isn't enough — the threat travels, it finds the next name, and the only real safety is making sure there is no next name to find.

I asked Merrick to stay not as a harbormaster calculating angles but as a man — and that terrifies me more than any customs inspector, because it means I've let someone matter before I've decided whether it's safe to.

beats.label: P5-close
beats.note: parallel to A's close; dramatic irony — HE kept every promise. The player didn't.
beats.location: the night dock, by the tackle-shed
beats.player: Because you kept every promise you ever made me, Corvin. Every one. A man doesn't let that kind bleed out on his own dock. ...And this time I'm not sailing anywhere.
beats.reply:
*He's still on the ground half-propped against the tackle-shed wall, and at that he goes very still — like a man who's misheard something too good to trust.*

Not sailing— 

*He wets his lips. Looks past you at the shape by the tackle, then back, and for once he doesn't finish the glance over his shoulder. He lets it land on you.*

You know what I am, Merrick. You've seen the crate, you've seen my name-burning, my— my tax rolls with a killer's name tucked in the customs figures. I'm a man the sea's trying to sweep clean, and every soul who's stood close to me ended up cold water or worse.

*His voice drops, cracked and quiet.*

And you're telling me you'd stay anyway. On *this* dock. With *me.*

...I don't— I've forgotten how to answer that. Nobody stays, Merrick. They pay, they board, they vanish. You're the first who ever turned round.

beats.note: closing deliberation, branch B: the save, the falsified assurance, the calm-water signature, the moved crate — all in one mind now

decision.reflection: Three things to weigh. First, asking Merrick to stay — not as a transaction but as a need: that's the most exposed I've been since I was young and stupid, and I haven't walked it back, which means some part of me has decided to stand there and take whatever comes. Second, the fire moving down the tackle-shed row — that reminder that danger doesn't stay put, it migrates; I've been passive long enough, believing that outlasting trouble was the same as ending it. Third, burning that last page and having him come back anyway, empty-handed, keeping his word for no gain at all — that's the proof I didn't know I was waiting my whole life for, and I don't know what to do with it except hold it very carefully.
decision.internal: He came back. Not for coin, not for leverage — he came back because I kept my promises and he considers that a reason. I've spent every year on this dock convinced that trust was a transaction waiting to go bad, and he keeps refusing to let it be that. The ask to stay — my ask — still sits in my chest like a stone I swallowed, but I'm not pulling it back. I'm not going to perform indifference and call it caution. He's earned more than that, and I think I've finally got enough proof to believe it without waiting for the catch.
decision.new_intent: Stop bracing for him to leave and start letting him be here — actually here, in the life, not just the trouble
new_goals: Stay off every ledger but my own until the last thread of Merrick's old business is cold and confirmed gone
Hide a second copy of what I know somewhere the inspector and anyone else can't reach — insurance I keep regardless of how safe I feel
Keep my ear to the harbor violence and track whether it's truly dispersing now the paymaster is cold, or migrating to a new name
Figure out what a life looks like when someone stays in it — and don't sabotage it out of habit
decision.world_action: Corvin moves to the far end of the fish-dock, checks over his shoulder once — old reflex — then sits down on the mooring post where the lamplight barely reaches, and does nothing for a long moment. He takes out the small folded paper he's kept inside his coat all week — blank, never written on — turns it over in his hands, and then deliberately tucks it back rather than reaching for a pen. Not every night needs a ledger entry. He sits, and waits, and lets himself.

beliefs: Anyone who asks to disappear from a manifest is either useful to me or dangerous — and until I know which, I keep them close and give away nothing.
A man with a killing purpose is safer to deal with than a man with a buying one — killers just need to get close, they don't need to rob you on the way out.
I've traded the crate for a name and a promise, and now the only leverage I have left is that page in my ledger — which means I've bet everything on Merrick Vale being the kind of man who comes back.

I burned the last page that bound him to me, and he still came back empty-handed — which means some men can actually be trusted, and I've been starving so long I'd almost forgotten what one looked like.

The fire moving down the tackle-shed row tells me that outlasting danger isn't enough — the threat travels, it finds the next name, and the only real safety is making sure there is no next name to find.

I asked Merrick to stay not as a harbormaster calculating angles but as a man — and that terrifies me more than any customs inspector, because it means I've let someone matter before I've decided whether it's safe to.
